pedagogy.summary: The 0-to-1 probability scale formalises chance as a measured quantity: every probability is a number from 0 (impossible) through 1/2 (even chance) to 1 (certain), and can be written as a fraction, decimal, or percentage. The teaching aim is to treat probability as a magnitude on a bounded number line — placing events, converting freely between the three notations, and connecting 0.5 back to the informal 'even chance'.
bestPractices: Anchor a single 0-to-1 line marked with the landmarks 0 (impossible), 1/2 (even chance), 1 (certain) and use it as the home for every probability
Show the SAME point written three ways — 1/2 = 0.5 = 50% — so children see the notations as one magnitude, not three separate things
Move both directions: from a described event to a position, and from a position back to a described likelihood
Stress the bounds: nothing can be less likely than impossible (0) or more likely than certain (1), so a probability can never be negative or exceed 1
Reconnect 0.5 to 'even chance' and small values to 'unlikely', linking the numeric scale to the words learned earlier
keyRepresentations: 0-to-1 number line with 0, 1/2, 1 landmarks (impossible / even / certain)
Triple-notation labels (fraction = decimal = percentage) at each position
Event cards placed along the line
Links from likelihood words to numeric positions
commonMisconceptions: Believing a probability can be greater than 1, or giving a probability as a raw count (e.g. '6' because a die has six outcomes)
Fraction interference — thinking a larger denominator means a larger probability (1/4 > 1/2 because 4 > 2)
Comparing mixed notations by surface digits without converting (ranking 40%, 1/4, 0.3 as 40 > 4 > 0.3)
Treating 0.5 / 'even chance' as the default for any two-outcome event

learn.summary: Teach probability as a magnitude on a bounded 0-to-1 line, with landmarks 0 (impossible), 1/2 (even chance) and 1 (certain). The same probability can be written three ways — fraction, decimal and percentage (1/2 = 0.5 = 50%) — and children should move both directions: from a described event to a position, and from a position back to a described likelihood. Stress the bounds (never below 0 or above 1) and reconnect 0.5 to the informal 'even chance' learned earlier. Comparing mixed notations requires converting to a common form, not ranking by surface digits or by denominator size.

activities.title: One position, three notations on a draggable scale
feedback: When the three notations appear together at one point, point out: these are not three different chances but one position written three ways.
If the learner expects '2' to be placeable, note that the scale stops at 1 because nothing is more likely than certain — a probability can never be a raw count like 6.
Blocking the drag past 0 and 1 makes the bounds felt directly; name them as impossible and certain as the marker reaches each end.
activities.rationale: Showing the same point as fraction, decimal and percentage at once targets the core idea that these notations are one magnitude. Blocking movement past the endpoints makes the bounds concrete and confronts the belief that a probability can exceed 1 or be a count. The live three-way readout and snap-to-line examples are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory.
sourceClaims: Probability is represented on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain) and expressed as a fraction, decimal or percentage; the same probability can be written in each of these forms.
learnerActions: Drag a marker along a 0-to-1 line; a readout shows wherever you land simultaneously as a fraction, a decimal AND a percentage, so 2/5, 0.4 and 40% appear together at the same point.
Place the 'chance of rain 40%' event and watch the marker coincide exactly with 0.4 and 2/5 — confirm these are one position written three ways, not three different chances.
Feed a computed probability from a bag or spinner and watch it snap onto the line at its matching position.
Try to shove the marker past the 'certain' end for a 'probability of 2' and notice it refuses to move beyond 1.
activities.intendedInsight: A probability is a single magnitude on a bounded line; the fraction, decimal and percentage are three ways of writing the same position, and nothing can be less likely than impossible (0) or more likely than certain (1).

activities.title: Place, order and match mixed-notation probabilities
feedback: If a learner ranks 40% > 1/4 > 0.3 by surface digits, convert all three to decimals (0.4, 0.25, 0.3) or mark them on the line; show 1/4 = 0.25 sitting below 0.3.

If a learner treats 1/4 as largest because of the 4 in the denominator, return to meaning: one part out of four is a smaller share than one part out of two; mark quarters and halves on the same line to compare.

For a value above 1 or below 0, re-anchor the bounds: nothing is more likely than certain (1) or less likely than impossible (0). When outcomes are equally likely, probability is favourable-over-total; the favourable count can never exceed the total or be negative, so the probability is at most 1 and never below 0.
activities.rationale: Placement, ordering and matching tasks rehearse exactly the conversions and placements the topic demands. Requiring conversion to a common form targets the documented tendency to fall back on additive or surface-number comparisons. The ordering answer 1/4=0.25, 0.3, 0.4 was checked: 0.25 < 0.3 < 0.4 is correct.
sourceClaims: Quantifying and comparing probabilities requires proportional reasoning; children commonly fall back on additive or surface-number comparisons rather than converting to a common proportion, a persistent difficulty documented across the probability literature.
learnerActions: Use a slider to place 1/4 and 0.7 on the 0-to-1 line.
Order 40%, 1/4 and 0.3 from least to most likely, converting each to a common form (decimals 0.25, 0.3, 0.4) before deciding.
Spot and reject an impossible probability, such as a value greater than 1 or below 0, explaining why it cannot be a valid probability.
activities.intendedInsight: Comparing probabilities written in different notations requires converting to a common form (decimals, or positions on the line); surface digits and denominator size are not reliable guides, and every valid probability lies between 0 and 1.

activities.title: Landmark reference line with revealed equivalents
feedback: Confirm that 1/2, 0.5 and 50% all mark the even-chance midpoint, linking back to the informal word learned earlier.
Prompt the learner to supply their own event for 0 and for 1 to check they grasp impossible and certain.
activities.rationale: A fixed reference line with tap-to-reveal equivalents clearly presents the triple notation and links words to positions. As a reference it does not let the child test a mis-placement, so it supports but does not replace active placement work; this limit is recorded in constraints.
sourceClaims: Probability is represented on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain) and expressed as a fraction, decimal or percentage; the same probability can be written in each of these forms.
learnerActions: Tap each landmark (0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 1) to reveal its fraction, decimal and percentage.
At each landmark, read an everyday event that belongs there (e.g. an impossible event at 0, a certain event at 1, an even-chance event at 1/2).
Use the revealed values as a reference while completing placement and ordering tasks.
activities.intendedInsight: Each landmark on the scale has a fixed fraction/decimal/percentage identity and a matching kind of everyday event, giving a stable reference for the triple notation.

activities.title: Socratic probing of the bounds
feedback: When the learner says a value cannot be placed, name the reason: nothing is more likely than certain (1) or less likely than impossible (0).

Redirect a count answer ('6 because a die has six outcomes') to favourable-over-total for a fair die's equally likely outcomes: the number of favourable outcomes can never be more than the total, so the fraction is never more than 1 (for example, 6/6 = 1 means certain).

If the learner assumes every two-outcome event is an even chance, point out that 0.5 applies only when the two outcomes are equally likely; many two-outcome events (e.g. a biased spinner) are not 1/2.
activities.rationale: A Socratic challenge surfaces the greater-than-1, count, and even-chance-default misconceptions by asking the child to justify and locate claimed values and to test a tempting generalisation. Discussion raises the ideas, but placing magnitudes may be clearer when also shown on a line, so pair this with the draggable or reference activities rather than using it alone.
learnerActions: Respond to a prompt such as 'the probability is 6' or 'could a probability be 2?' by explaining what 0 and 1 mean.
Locate a claimed value like '6' or '2' on the 0-to-1 line and explain why it cannot sit there.
Describe an event at 0 (impossible) and an event at 1 (certain) in your own words.

Judge a claim like 'any event with two possible outcomes has probability 1/2' — decide whether it is always true, using an example such as a biased spinner or an event much more likely than its alternative.
activities.intendedInsight: Nothing is more likely than certain, so probability tops out at 1; a raw count of outcomes is not a probability; and 0.5 is the even-chance value only when the two outcomes are equally likely, not automatically for any two-outcome event.

constraints: The 0-to-1 probability scale is a one-dimensional magnitude; a line (physical, drawn or on screen) is the appropriate representation and no additional spatial dimension is needed.
A fixed reference line shows equivalents clearly but cannot let a child test a mis-placement, so it supports rather than replaces active placement, ordering and conversion work.

Dialogue/Socratic prompts can raise the bounds, count and even-chance-default misconceptions, but should be paired with actually placing values on a line, since placing magnitudes may be clearer when shown.

Matching and recognising equivalent forms is useful practice, but is recognition-level; include tasks where the child independently places and orders values and states a reason, not only selects from options.
Mixed-notation comparison must require conversion to a common form; do not accept ordering by surface digits or by denominator size as correct reasoning.
0.5 ('even chance') is correct only when the two outcomes are equally likely; do not teach it as the default for every two-outcome event.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the ordering example: 1/4 = 0.25, 0.3, 40% = 0.4 gives least-to-most order A, B, C (0.25 < 0.3 < 0.4) — correct as stated. The listed distractors (40% > 1/4 > 0.3 by digits; 1/4 largest by denominator) are intentionally wrong patterns to diagnose and must only appear as error patterns, never as correct feedback.

The assessment's die example ('probability of rolling less than 7 on a six-sided die') is certain = 1; the count answer '6' is the targeted misconception. This is logically sound and preserved as the count/bounds-confrontation idea in the Socratic activity.

The 'even chance is the default for any two-outcome event' misconception appears only in the original pedagogy field, not among the formal assessment error patterns; it has been added as a conservative Socratic probe to preserve it. This addition is an unvalidated proposal.
Claims that one medium is clearer than another (e.g. shown vs discussed) are proposals only; efficacy is untested and such statements use 'may' wording.
Legacy source claims were marked verified in the row but have not been re-checked here; confidence should not be upgraded on that basis.

assess.poeTask: Say: 'I'm going to roll this fair six-sided die. What is the probability that I roll a number less than 7? Write it as a number and explain — and could it be more than 1?' Have the child predict AND justify before rolling. A child who thinks in counts answers '6' (six numbers are less than 7); the correct answer is 1 (certain). Roll the die several times — every roll is under 7 — to confront the count answer: the event is certain, which is 1 on the scale, and nothing can be 'more than certain'.
probeDeeper: Where does 'even chance' sit on this line, and what is it as a decimal and a percentage?
Could a probability ever be more than 1? What would that mean?
Is 1/4 the same as, bigger than, or smaller than 0.3? How can you be sure?
Point to 0 on the line — describe an event that belongs there, and one that belongs at 1.
assess.correctAnswer: Least to most likely: A (1/4 = 0.25), then B (0.3), then C (40% = 0.4). Converting all three to the same form — decimals 0.25, 0.3, 0.4, or positions on the line — shows the order; each sits between 0 and 1, with A a quarter of the way, B just above it, and C below the halfway point.

errorPatterns.pattern: Compares mixed notations by their surface digits without converting ('40 is biggest, then 4, then 0.3')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convert all three to a common form (decimals, or positions on the line) before comparing; show 1/4 = 0.25 sitting below 0.3
errorPatterns.distractor: C (40%), then A (1/4), then B (0.3) — 40 is the biggest number, then 4, then 0.3.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders by the raw numbers seen rather than their true magnitudes; may rank 1/4 above 0.3 by reading '4' as four

errorPatterns.pattern: Fraction interference — a bigger denominator is read as a bigger probability (1/4 > 1/2 because 4 > 2)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the meaning: one part out of four is a smaller share than one out of two; mark quarters and halves on the same line to compare their sizes
errorPatterns.distractor: A (1/4) is the most likely because it has the biggest bottom number.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places 1/4 high on the scale or calls it the most likely because of the 4 in the denominator

errorPatterns.pattern: Believes a probability can exceed 1 or gives it as a raw count (e.g. '6' for a die)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-anchor the bounds: nothing is more likely than certain, so probability tops out at 1; a probability is favourable-over-total, always at most the total, so never more than 1
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places a mark beyond the 'certain' end, or states a probability greater than 1 or as a whole number of outcomes

responseLevels.gap: Cannot place probabilities on the line or convert between notations; orders by surface digits and may put marks beyond 0 or 1
responseLevels.full: Converts freely between fraction, decimal and percentage, orders mixed-notation probabilities correctly, places each between 0 and 1, and rules out values below 0 or above 1 with a reason
responseLevels.partial: Places single-notation probabilities correctly and knows the endpoints, but slips when notations are mixed — compares by raw digits or by denominator size — or is unsure a probability cannot exceed 1

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show three events with their probabilities written in different notations: Event A has probability 1/4, Event B has probability 0.3, Event C has probability 40%. Ask the child to order them from least to most likely and to place each on a 0-to-1 line. Take the order, then ask them to explain the reason (Tier 2) — how they compared numbers written in different ways.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the scale converts to a common notation and places all three between 0 and 1; a surface reasoner ranks by the visible digits (40 > 4 > 3), and a fraction-interference reasoner treats 1/4 as large because of the 4. The Tier-2 reason — did they convert to compare? — is the separator, and only converted reasoning survives.
